about: Pope Sergius I (687–701) brought this acclamation into the Roman Mass: the Liber Pontificalis records that he ordered clergy and people to sing “Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccáta mundi, miserére nobis” while the Lord's Body is broken. The words are the Baptist's at the Jordan, but turned from report into address: the Gospel has “ecce qui tollit peccátum mundi” — third person, and sin in the singular — where the Mass says “qui tollis peccáta mundi”. The ending of the third invocation is not fixed: “dona nobis pacem” looks ahead to the kiss of peace, and where that kiss is not given the ending changes with it — “dona eis réquiem” at Masses for the dead, and a third “miserére nobis” on Holy Thursday.

s01.narrative: The priest covers the chalice, genuflects and rises. Bowing before the Blessed Sacrament with joined hands, he says the Agnus Dei in an audible voice and strikes his breast three times — at each “miserére nobis” and at “dona nobis pacem”. At a sung Mass the choir takes it up.

s02.translation: Lamb of God, you who take away the sins of the world: have mercy on us.

s03.translation: Lamb of God, you who take away the sins of the world: have mercy on us.

s04.translation: Lamb of God, you who take away the sins of the world: grant us peace.

s05.narrative: This rubric governs Masses for the dead: there “dona eis réquiem” takes the place of “miserére nobis”, and the third time “dona eis réquiem sempitérnam”. At those Masses the priest does not strike his breast, and the kiss of peace is not given.

w001.function: A nominative doing a vocative's work — Latin's habit in solemn apostrophes; the vocative proper would be “agne”. The Gloria carries the same phrase: “Dómine Deus, Agnus Dei”.

w004.function: Second person singular: the words go straight to the Lamb, not about him — hence “you take away”, not “he takes away”. The address the relative reaches back to is “Agnus” (w001).

w023.function: An imperative with two objects: the thing in the accusative — “pacem” (w025), the person in the dative — “nobis” (w024). This is the one place where the third invocation parts from the first two.
